title_en: The Sharia Sciences Series — Tape Five
body_ar: *أبدع تمام بيان لاختصارك في ** جمع ورتب وأصلح يا أخي الخللا* فقوله "أبدع" هذا هو المقصد الأول من مقاصد التأليف أن يأتي الإنسان بجديد لم يسبق إليه، والجديد نسبي لأنه بالإمكان أن يكون قد تعرض له شخص في موضع من المواضع أو تكلم عليه في مكان ما ، لكن فتح أمامك أنت ذلك بابا واسعا ، أو أعطاك خيوطا يمكن أن تصل بها إلى غير هذا فالإبداع نسبي دائما ، ولهذا تجدون كثيرا من أهل العلم يقولون فيما من الله عليهم به من الفتوحات الربانية، يقولون ولم أسبق إلى مثل هذا ، يقول بن العربي رحمه الله عندما يورد مسألة من المسائل الفقهية النادرة أو الأصولية ، يقول: قلت وهذا علم ما شم المالكية رائحته، ولا تجاوز بلخ وخراسان لأنه من علوم المشارقة ما وصل إلى المغرب نهائيا ، هو أول من أوصله ، يقول ما شم أصحابنا رائحة هذه المسألة قبلي ، لم تتعد بلخ وخراسان ..
body_en:
*Create anew; complete; expound; and for your abridging — collect, arrange, and set right, my brother, the flaw.*

His words "create anew": this is the first of the aims of authorship, that a person bring something new to which no one has gone before him. And "new" is relative, because it is possible that someone has touched upon it in one place or another, or spoken about it somewhere; but that opened a wide door before you, or gave you threads by which you could reach something beyond it. So origination is always relative. For this reason you find many of the people of knowledge saying, of what God has favoured them with of divine openings, they say: "and I have not been preceded to the like of this". Ibn al-'Arabi — may God have mercy on him — says, when he brings up one of the rare juristic questions or one of the questions of legal theory (uṣūl), he says: "I say: this is a knowledge whose scent the Malikis have not smelled, and it has not passed beyond Balkh and Khurasan" — because it is among the sciences of the easterners; it had not reached the Maghrib at all, and he is the first to bring it there. He says: our colleagues have not smelled the scent of this question before me; it has not gone beyond Balkh and Khurasan..

flags.arabic: يقول بن العربي ـ رحمه الله ـ
flags.context: the scholar quoted on rare Maliki juristic and usuli questions
options: Qadi Abu Bakr Ibn al-'Arabi al-Ma'afiri, the Maliki jurist of Seville (d. 543/1148)
Muhyi al-Din Ibn 'Arabi, the Andalusian Sufi (d. 638/1240)
flags.note: CRITICAL for the English reader. The source writes 'بن العربي' without the alif of 'ابن'. In English, 'Ibn Arabi' unqualified is read as the Sufi Muhyi al-Din, who is a different man and a contested figure. Everything in the context — rare Maliki juristic questions, questions of legal theory, 'our colleagues' meaning the Malikis, the eastern sciences reaching the Maghrib — points to Qadi Abu Bakr Ibn al-'Arabi, the Maliki jurist. The English keeps the definite article ('Ibn al-'Arabi') to mark the distinction, but the record should carry the full name before publication. Confusing the two would misattribute a Sufi metaphysician's authority to a point of Maliki legal method.

flags.note: A mnemonic verse enumerating the recognised aims of composing a book: origination, completing an incomplete work, expounding an obscure one, abridging a long one, collecting what is scattered, arranging, and correcting error. The Sheikh comments only on the first of them within this excerpt, so the English does not name the others beyond what the line itself says. The asterisks around and between the hemistichs are the source's own verse markers, not emphasis, and are not reproduced in the English. Rendered as prose in italics per style guide section 4.

translator_notes: A course lesson on the aims of authorship. No legal ruling is given anywhere in it.
'الفتوحات الربانية' is rendered 'divine openings' in its ordinary sense of insight granted to a scholar; it carries no reference here to the Sufi work of the same root.
